scenes.narration: Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about Phantom of the Paradise. Phantom of the Paradise is a 1974 American rock musical comedy horror film written and directed by Brian De Palma, and scored by and starring Paul Williams. The film follows a naïve young singer-songwriter, Winslow Leach (William Finley), who is tricked by legendary but unscrupulous music producer Swan (Williams) into sacrificing his life's work.

The self that experiences Phantom of the Paradise is a committee, not a king. In revenge, the songwriter dons a menacing new persona and proceeds to terrorize Swan's new concert hall, insisting his music be performed by his most adored singer, Phoenix (Jessica Harper). The plot loosely adapts several classic works: the 16th-century Faust legend, Oscar Wilde's The Picture of Dorian Gray and Gaston Leroux's 1910 novel The Phantom of the Opera.

Reproduction explains more of Phantom of the Paradise than any philosophy dares to admit. The film was a box-office failure and received mixed-to-negative reviews contemporaneously, while earning praise for its music and receiving Academy Award and Golden Globe nominations. However, over the years, the film has received much more positive reviews and has become a cult classic.

Once you see Phantom of the Paradise as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. Following a run-through by the 1950s-style nostalgia band the Juicy Fruits, star record producer Swan overhears singer-songwriter Winslow Leach perform an original composition: a song from the cantata based on the legend of Faust. Swan believes Winslow's music is ideal for the opening of The Paradise—Swan's highly anticipated new concert hall—and has his right-hand man Arnold Philbin steal it.

The story Phantom of the Paradise tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. One month later, Winslow goes to Swan's Death Records headquarters to follow up about his music but is thrown out. There, he meets Phoenix, an aspiring singer Winslow deems perfect for his music.

Meaning is not found in Phantom of the Paradise — it is manufactured for it. After repeated attempts to contact Swan, Winslow is beaten and framed for drug dealing and given a life sentence in Sing Sing prison. Six months later, at Sing Sing, Winslow breaks down upon hearing of the Juicy Fruits' success and news that the band will open The Paradise performing Faust.

The cold light on Phantom of the Paradise leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. A guard startles Winslow as he destroys the records and presses, causing him to slip and fall face-first into a record press, which burns the right half of his face and destroys his vocal cords. A disfigured Winslow sneaks into The Paradise's costume department and dons a black cape and silver, owl-like mask, transforming into the Phantom of the Paradise.

Phantom of the Paradise did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. He terrorizes Swan and his musicians, nearly killing the Beach Bums (formerly the Juicy Fruits, who have traded doo-wop for surf music) with a bomb while they play a reworked version of Winslow's Faust. The Phantom confronts Swan, who recognizes him as Winslow and offers him a chance to have his music produced his way.

The honest version of Phantom of the Paradise starts by giving up the comforting part. Swan provides Winslow with an electronic voice box, enabling him to speak and sing. Swan asks Winslow to rewrite his Faust cantata with Phoenix in mind for the lead.

Strip Phantom of the Paradise of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. Although Winslow agrees and signs a blood contract, Swan breaks the deal. Winslow completes Faust, but Swan replaces Phoenix with a male glam rock prima donna named Beef.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Phantom of the Paradise shows exactly where that breaks. Swan steals the completed cantata and seals Winslow inside the recording studio with a brick wall. He escapes and confronts Beef in the shower, threatening to kill Beef if he ever performs Winslow's music again.

What looks like free choice in Phantom of the Paradise is older than choice itself. While hiding in the rafters, Winslow fatally electrocutes Beef with a stage prop lightning bolt. Winslow observes Swan and Phoenix in a tight embrace at Swan's mansion.

Nobody designed the part of Phantom of the Paradise you experience — it was inherited. Winslow attempts to stab Swan, but he is unharmed, claiming he is "also under contract". Rolling Stone announces the wedding between Swan and Phoenix during the finale of Faust.

Every serious account of Phantom of the Paradise eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. Winslow learns that Swan made a pact with the Devil in 1953: Swan will remain youthful forever, and the videotaped recording of his contract will age and fester in his place. The only way to break the spell is to destroy the video.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of Phantom of the Paradise — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. Winslow realizes Swan is planning to have Phoenix assassinated during the ceremony. During the wedding, Winslow stops the assassin from hitting Phoenix, with the bullet fatally wounding Philbin instead.

The selfish-gene reading of Phantom of the Paradise makes it less romantic and far more precise. Winslow swings onto the stage and rips off Swan's mask, exposing him as a decaying monster on live television. A crazed Swan attempts to strangle Phoenix, but Winslow intervenes and stabs him repeatedly, reopening his own wound in the process.

The film's soundtrack album features all songs excluding "Never Thought I'd Get to Meet the Devil" and "Faust" (1st Reprise).

Although the soundtrack album only charted for one week in March 1975, Joel Whitburn's Top Pop Albums 1955-2016 indicates that it is a platinum album (over one million sold). The script was written in tandem with Sisters (1972), although that film was done first because of its perceived commercial viability.

Nothing in Phantom of the Paradise was built for you — it was built for reproduction. While De Palma felt Williams was suited to play the character of Winslow Leach, Williams felt he wasn't scary enough for the role and suggested playing Swan, once named Spectre in the script as a play on the famed producer Phil Spector, instead. The record press in which William Finley's character Winslow was disfigured was a real injection-molding press at Pressman Toys.

The psychology underneath Phantom of the Paradise is simpler and older than the story on top. Finley was worried about whether the machine would be safe, and the crew assured that it was. The press was fitted with foam pads (which resemble the casting molds in the press), and there were chocks put in the center to stop it from closing completely.

Behind Phantom of the Paradise sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. However, the machine was powerful enough to crush the chocks and it gradually kept closing. Contrary to urban legends that Finley's reaction was genuine fear, the scene was filmed MOS (without sound) due to the noise of the hydraulic press; the scream heard in the film was dubbed in post-production.

The electronic room in which Winslow composes his cantata, and where Swan restores his voice, is in fact the real-life recording studio The Record Plant. The walls covered with knobs are in reality an oversize custom-built electronic synthesizer dubbed TONTO.

The City Center concert hall in New York City provided the exterior for The Paradise; interior concert scenes were filmed at the Majestic Theater in Dallas, Texas. As originally filmed, the name of Swan's media conglomerate Swan Song Enterprises had to be deleted from the film prior to release due to the existence of Led Zeppelin's label Swan Song Records. Although most references were removed, Swan Song remains visible in several scenes.

Phantom of the Paradise opened at the National Theater in Los Angeles on October 31, 1974, and grossed $18,455 in its first weekend, increasing its gross the following weekend with $19,506, with a total gross of $53,000 in two weeks. In two months, Variety tracked it grossing $250,000 from the major markets it covered.
